_readme: Unit 10: conditionals and the unreal past. Ten points, authored as TWO SYSTEMS rather than four numbered types, per DESIGN.md section 0.5 override 5: the real system (gr_cond_zero, gr_cond_first, gr_cond_first_uses, gr_cond_alternatives) and the unreal system, which is one distancing mechanism (gr_unreal_past) spent six times over gr_cond_second, gr_cond_second_uses, gr_cond_third, gr_cond_mixed and gr_wish_family. The numbers 0/1/2/3 are kept as labels applied afterwards, because learners arrive holding them.

gr_unreal_past is the organising principle and is authored as a hard prerequisite of gr_cond_second, gr_cond_third and gr_wish_family, exactly as override 5 requires. Its teaching claim - that a backward step marks distance from reality rather than distance in time - is stated in our own words and is not lifted from any source.

This block key is not one of the six in DESIGN.md section 4.1; the orchestrator re-split G-A5's unreal-clauses allocation and u11 and u13 are owned by sibling blocks. All ten point ids are taken verbatim from the closed set in DESIGN.md section 4.2 and none is invented. Four cross-block prerequisites are referenced and not renamed: gr_present_simple, gr_sub_time, gr_future_will, gr_future_time_clause, gr_past_simple_regular, gr_past_perfect, gr_modal_grammar and gr_modal_perfect.

vocab_new and vocab_updates are deliberately empty: DESIGN.md section 4.1 allocates vocabulary decks to G-A1..G-A6, this block has no deck allocation, and the sibling staging file vocabulary-expansion.json owns the vocabulary push, so authoring entries here would risk id collisions.

points.title: Stating what always happens once a condition is met

teach.can_do: I can state a rule: once this is true, that follows, every time.
teach.why_it_matters: Describing a machine, a rule or a natural process needs this shape, and it is the cheapest two-part sentence English has.
teach.meaning: Some sentences are not reports about one occasion. They are claims about what the world reliably does. Put the tide below the marker and the ferry cannot dock — that is not a guess about Tuesday, it is a standing fact about the slipway. This shape allows no exceptions: it says that on every single occasion the first half is true, the second half follows. That is why it fits rules, machinery, procedures and natural processes, and why it sounds odd for a one-off.

notes: The two halves can swap places: the ferry cannot dock if the tide drops below the marker. When the if half comes second, no comma is needed.
When means almost exactly the same thing here, because you are talking about every occasion rather than one of them.
The if half never takes will, even though the sentence covers tomorrow as well as today.
form.negative: If the pump does not restart within a minute, the tank overflows.
form.question: What happens if the tide drops below the marker?

left.role: the condition, in a present form
left.text: If the tide drops below the marker

right.role: what follows, every occasion, also in a present form

spec.caption: No guess about one afternoon. A standing claim about every afternoon.

worked_example.sentence: If the river rises above the flood wall, the pumping station shuts itself down.
worked_example.why_this_form: Nothing is being predicted. The station is built so that this happens on every occasion the water gets that high, and both halves stay in a present form to say so.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting will into the second half would turn a standing fact about the station into a forecast about one particular flood the speaker has in mind.

notice_set.sentence: If the tide drops below the marker, the ferry cannot dock.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker talking about one particular afternoon?
notice_set.why: The sentence is describing how the slipway behaves, so it covers every afternoon the water gets that low.

notice_set.sentence: If the sample is left in daylight, the colour fades inside a day.
notice_set.question: Would the colour fade on a sample left out next month?
notice_set.why: A rule about samples carries forward. Next month's sample is covered by it without being mentioned.

notice_set.sentence: If the outside air falls below about minus five, the backup heater takes over.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know whether it will be that cold tonight?
notice_set.why: The sentence is about the heating system, not about tonight. Tonight has not been mentioned at all.

notice_set.sentence: If you do not rinse the rice, it sticks to the base of the pan.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving a warning about one particular meal?
notice_set.why: This is what rice does. Nobody's dinner tonight is being discussed.

notice_set.sentence: The gritters go out at four if the road surface freezes overnight.
notice_set.question: Is this what the council does every cold night, or only tonight?
notice_set.why: Both halves stay in a present form, which is how English says that this is the standing arrangement.

discovery.prompt: Two of these describe how something always behaves. One is about a single occasion. Work out what tells you which is which.
pairs: If the tide drops below the marker, the ferry cannot dock.
If the tide drops below the marker tonight, the ferry will stay out.
If you do not rinse the rice, it sticks to the base of the pan.
If you do not rinse this rice, it will stick to the pan.
The gritters go out at four if the road surface freezes overnight.
The gritters will go out at four if the road freezes tonight.

candidate_rules.text: On the left both halves stay in a present form because the sentence covers every occasion, not one.
The left-hand sentences are about machines and weather, and the right-hand ones are about people.
Whenever a sentence contains the word if, the second half needs will.

teach.rule_line: Ask: is this true every time, or only this time?
teach.false_rule: That if points at the future and therefore drags will in behind it. Here if points at every occasion, and will has nothing to add.

errors.wrong: If the temperature will fall below zero, the sensors stop reporting.
errors.right: If the temperature falls below zero, the sensors stop reporting.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reads the sentence as being about the future, and English usually marks the future with will, so it lands in the first half where nothing needs it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will fall becomes falls.

errors.wrong: If the tank would fill past the upper mark, the overflow pipe opens.
errors.right: If the tank fills past the upper mark, the overflow pipe opens.
errors.why_it_happens: Would has been stored as the word that keeps if company, so it arrives on its own. Nothing here is being imagined; the sentence is describing what the tank does.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would fill becomes fills.

errors.wrong: If the pressure drops below two bar. The valve closes automatically.
errors.right: If the pressure drops below two bar, the valve closes automatically.
errors.why_it_happens: The first half is long enough to feel finished, so a full stop arrives. On its own it names a condition and never says what follows from it, which leaves the reader waiting.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one punctuation mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

pays_in.note: Nearly every process description states what happens at a stage once a condition is met.
pays_in.model: If the salt content rises too far, the membrane is flushed and the cycle begins again.

pays_in.note: Science passages state their mechanisms in this shape and questions turn on them.
pays_in.model: If the surface water cools quickly enough, the layers beneath it stop mixing.

pays_in.note: Explaining how something normally works is a Part 3 staple.
pays_in.model: If a town loses its last bank, older residents stop going into the centre altogether.

used_in.quote: A process diagram is a chain of conditions, and describing it without this shape means writing every stage twice.
The passage explains a mechanism, and one question depends on reading a stated rule as a rule rather than as an event.

payload.sentence: If the barrier is down, the level crossing lights stay red.
payload.question: Is this about one particular morning?

feedback.why_key: Both halves sit in a present form, which is how English says that this is how the crossing behaves on every occasion.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the sentence as a claim about all occasions before you look for a date.

payload.sentence: If a soil sample dries out completely, the count of living organisms in it collapses.
payload.question: Would the same thing happen to a sample collected next spring?

feedback.why_key: The sentence is a claim about soil samples in general, so it reaches forward to samples nobody has collected yet.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the claim covers cases the sentence never names.

payload.context: From a description of how a flood scheme is meant to work.
payload.sentence: If the water level will rise above the wall, the pumping station shuts itself down.
reasons: the first half is describing every occasion, so it needs no will
the pumping station has not been built yet
the halves have been written the wrong way round
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The sentence is describing a permanent arrangement, and will would narrow it to one flood the writer has in mind.
feedback.feed_forward: Take will out of the if half whenever you are stating a rule.

payload.context: From a note on how a heat pump behaves in cold weather.
payload.stem: If the outside air ___ (fall) below about minus five, the backup heater takes over.

feedback.why_key: This is what the system does every cold night, so the first half stays in its plain present form.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the if half present when you are describing normal behaviour.

payload.context: From a card pinned above a bakery worktop.
payload.stem: If you ___ (not chill) the dough first, the biscuits spread right across the tray.

feedback.why_key: The negative changes nothing about the shape. Both halves keep a present form because this is what dough does.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the negative on do, then leave the rest of the sentence alone.

payload.context: Two colleagues comparing morning routines.
payload.stem: If I ___ (skip) breakfast, I get a headache by about eleven.

feedback.why_key: The speaker is describing what her body reliably does, not planning tomorrow morning.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the plain present when you are describing your own regular pattern.

payload.context: Build one sentence about what happens on still evenings near the Verdon works.

expected: if the wind drops the smoke settles over the valley
the smoke settles over the valley if the wind drops

feedback.why_key: Both orders are ordinary English and mean the same thing. Only the punctuation changes when the if half moves to the back.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the two halves in either order, then check that both have a verb.

payload.given: Ice forms on the overhead wires. The trains then run at half speed all day.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that states this as a standing rule rather than as news.

expected: forms on the overhead wires the trains run at half speed all day
forms on the overhead wires, the trains run at half speed all day
forms on the overhead wires the trains run at half speed
forms on the overhead wires, the trains run at half speed

feedback.why_key: Folding the two into one turns a report about a particular morning into a claim about every icy morning.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the condition to the result and keep both verbs in a present form.

payload.audio_text: If you don't rinse the rice, it sticks to the pan.

expected: if you don't rinse the rice it sticks to the pan
if you do not rinse the rice it sticks to the pan
if you dont rinse the rice it sticks to the pan

feedback.why_key: Don't and sticks are both squeezed almost flat in speech, and a listener who misses them hears a completely different claim.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small ending on the second verb, not just the first.

payload.context: From a paragraph explaining a safety valve.
payload.sentence: If the pressure would drop below two bar, the valve closes automatically.
reasons: nothing is being imagined here, so would has no work to do
the valve is described in the wrong half
the sentence needs a full stop rather than a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Would tells a reader that a situation is being imagined. This valve really does close, several times a week.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete would from the if half when the sentence states a fact.

payload.sentence: If a road surface will freeze overnight, the gritters go out at four in the morning.

feedback.why_key: The second half already tells you this is the standing arrangement, so the first half must describe every cold night too.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the two halves: if one states a rule, so must the other.

payload.prompt_text: A recycling scheme only collects glass from households that put the bin out before seven. Write one sentence stating what happens, every week, to a household that misses that time.

feedback.why_key: Stating the rule once is what lets a reader work out every particular case without being told about each one.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the rule, not the story of one household.

payload.prompt_text: Take the process answer you wrote about turning sea water into drinking water. Rewrite one stage so that it states what happens on every occasion the salt level climbs too high. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A process answer that never states a condition has to list occasions instead, and it runs out of words before it runs out of stages.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace one listed event with the rule behind it.

points.title: Saying what will follow if something that might happen does happen

teach.can_do: I can say what will follow if something I think might really happen does happen.
teach.why_it_matters: Argument is mostly this shape. You cannot say a policy will work without saying what happens if it is brought in.
teach.meaning: Here the speaker is not describing a rule. They have one particular future occasion in mind and they genuinely do not know how it will go. The first half puts a real possibility on the table: the strike may go ahead, the funding may arrive, the water may rise again. The second half says what the speaker expects to follow from it. The whole sentence is a bet the speaker is prepared to make, which is why it carries weight in an argument.

notes: In the second half, may, might, can, should and an instruction all work in place of will: if the alarm sounds, leave by the side door.
In speech will is almost always squeezed down to 'll, and it disappears entirely if you are not listening for it.
The halves can swap: the depot will close for two days if the strike goes ahead.
form.negative: If the funding does not arrive by June, the centre will stay shut.
form.question: What will happen if the strike goes ahead?

ends: I think this could really happen

marks.label: If the strike goes ahead, the depot will close.
If the strike goes ahead, the depot may close.
reserved for the shape taught later in this unit

worked_example.sentence: If the reservoir drops below a quarter full, the council will bring in a hosepipe ban.
worked_example.why_this_form: The speaker has this summer in mind and does not know how dry it will get. The drop is a live possibility, and the ban is what they expect to follow from it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting the second half into a present form would turn this into a standing rule of the council's, true every year, rather than a forecast about the summer in front of them.

notice_set.sentence: If the strike goes ahead, the depot will close for two days.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know whether the strike is happening?
notice_set.why: Putting the strike after if is how the speaker says it is still open. If it were settled they would not have hedged it.

notice_set.sentence: If the funding arrives before June, the centre will open in September.
notice_set.question: Is the centre opening in September?
notice_set.why: The opening has been tied to the money. Nothing has been promised about the money.

notice_set.sentence: The path will stay shut if the tide comes over the wall again.
notice_set.question: Has the tide come over the wall before?
notice_set.why: Again is doing quiet work: it tells you this has happened at least once already, which is why the speaker treats it as a live risk.

notice_set.sentence: If the bus is late, ring the office and someone will come out for you.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving an instruction or making a prediction?
notice_set.why: The second half tells you what to do and then what to expect. Both live comfortably after if.

notice_set.sentence: If nobody objects by Friday, the plan goes to the committee.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker talking about one particular Friday?
notice_set.why: A named deadline pins the sentence to one occasion, and that is what separates this from a standing rule.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same words about the same situation. Work out what the speaker on the right is doing differently.
pairs: If the reservoir drops below a quarter full, the council brings in a hosepipe ban.
If the reservoir drops below a quarter full, the council will bring in a hosepipe ban.
If the tide comes over the wall, the coast path shuts.
If the tide comes over the wall again, the coast path will shut.
If nobody objects, a plan goes to the committee.
If nobody objects by Friday, the plan goes to the committee.

candidate_rules.text: The right-hand speaker has one particular occasion in mind and is saying what they expect on it.
The right-hand sentences are the polite versions.
A sentence needs will as soon as it mentions a day of the week.

teach.rule_line: One occasion you cannot call yet: keep if plain and let will do the predicting.
teach.false_rule: That a sentence about the future needs will in both halves. Only the half that predicts takes it; the half that supposes stays plain.

errors.wrong: If the strike will go ahead, the depot will close for two days.
errors.right: If the strike goes ahead, the depot will close for two days.
errors.why_it_happens: The whole sentence is about the future, so the learner marks the future in both halves. English marks it once, in the half doing the predicting, and treats the supposing half as settled ground.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will go becomes goes.
errors.l1_note: Plenty of languages put a marker of futurity inside the condition as well, so the habit arrives fully formed.

errors.wrong: If the funding would arrive in time, the centre will open in September.
errors.right: If the funding arrives in time, the centre will open in September.
errors.why_it_happens: Would has been learned as a softener, and the learner is being cautious about money nobody has promised. The caution is already carried by if, and would drags the sentence into imagining instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would arrive becomes arrives.

errors.wrong: If the council approved the scheme, work will start in April.
errors.right: If the council approves the scheme, work will start in April.
errors.why_it_happens: A past form has been reached for to signal doubt, but the second half still predicts flatly. The two halves now disagree about whether any of this is expected to happen.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: approved becomes approves.

pays_in.note: A body paragraph arguing for a policy is a chain of these sentences.
pays_in.model: If councils charge for parking in the centre, shoppers will simply drive to the retail parks instead.

pays_in.note: Part 3 asks what will happen next, and the honest answer is conditional.
pays_in.model: If house prices keep climbing, younger people will just stop moving out of their parents' homes.

pays_in.note: Arrangements in Part 1 recordings arrive as conditions, with the detail parked after the comma.
pays_in.model: If the coach is full, we'll put on a second one at half past.

used_in.quote: Arguing about free transport means saying what will follow if fares are abolished, which is this shape used ten times over.
Every follow-up on this card asks what happens next, and none of it can be answered flatly.

payload.question: Does the speaker know whether the strike is happening?

feedback.why_key: Putting the strike after if is how a speaker says it is still open. Somebody who knew would not have hedged it.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat what sits after if as something still undecided.

payload.sentence: If the grant arrives before June, the evening classes will run again from September.
payload.question: Are the evening classes running in September?

feedback.why_key: The classes have been tied to the money, and nothing at all has been promised about the money.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace what the promise is hanging on before you treat it as news.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about land for new homes.
payload.sentence: If the government will build on green land, small towns will lose the fields around them.
reasons: the half that supposes should stay plain
the two halves are about different countries
the sentence needs a full stop rather than a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: English marks the future once, in the half that predicts. The half after if is treated as settled ground for the sake of argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip will out of the if half and leave the plain verb.

payload.context: From a note circulated before a dry summer.
payload.stem: If the reservoir ___ (drop) below a quarter full, the council will bring in a hosepipe ban.

feedback.why_key: The ban is the prediction; the drop is the supposition, and English keeps suppositions plain.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb after if in its plain present form.

payload.context: From a letter about a proposed park-and-ride site.
payload.stem: If the site opens next spring, traffic through the village ___ (fall) sharply.

feedback.why_key: The writer thinks the site really may open, so the second half is a forecast about one particular spring.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the prediction in the half that is not after if.

payload.context: A supervisor on the phone to a driver.
payload.stem: If the yard ___ (be) still blocked at six, take the load round to the Ashfield gate.

feedback.why_key: An instruction sits perfectly happily where a prediction would go, and it leaves the first half untouched.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the if half plain even when the second half is an order.

payload.given: The clinic may lose one of its two nurses. Waiting times would then double.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence treating the loss as something that could genuinely happen this year.

expected: loses one of its two nurses waiting times will double
loses one of its two nurses, waiting times will double
loses one of its two nurses waiting times will double this year
loses one of its two nurses, waiting times will double this year

feedback.why_key: Treating the loss as real is what turns a piece of speculation into a warning somebody can act on.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the supposition plain and let will carry the consequence.

payload.context: Build one sentence for an essay about the cost of public transport.

expected: if fares rise again passengers will drift back to cars
passengers will drift back to cars if fares rise again

feedback.why_key: Whichever half comes first, will stays with the consequence and never crosses into the supposition.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the halves freely, but leave will where it started.

payload.audio_text: If the coach is full, we'll put on a second one at half past.

expected: if the coach is full we'll put on a second one at half past
if the coach is full we will put on a second one at half past
if the coach is full well put on a second one at half past

feedback.why_key: We'll and we sound almost identical at speed, and losing the 'll turns a plan into a claim about now.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a soft l riding on the pronoun.

payload.context: From a first draft of a funding letter.
payload.sentence: If the grant would arrive in time, the centre will open in September.
reasons: the caution is already carried by if, so would pulls the sentence into imagining
the centre has already opened
September is too far away for this shape
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The second half still predicts flatly, so the two halves end up disagreeing about whether any of this is expected.
feedback.feed_forward: Let if do the hedging and keep the verb after it plain.

payload.sentence: If the council approved the scheme next month, work will start on the first block in April.

feedback.why_key: Next month and will start both treat this as a live plan, so the first half cannot quietly step back from reality.
feedback.feed_forward: Make both halves agree about whether this is expected.

payload.prompt_text: A town is considering scrapping bus fares altogether next year. Write one sentence saying what you expect to follow if it goes ahead.

feedback.why_key: Naming the consequence is what turns an opinion about a policy into an argument a reader can weigh.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what follows, not whether you like it.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked what would help most with air quality in your nearest city. In forty-five seconds, name one measure and say what you expect to follow if it is actually brought in.

feedback.why_key: An answer that names a measure and stops is half an answer. The consequence is the part that shows you have thought about it.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the measure, then finish the sentence with what follows.

points.title: Choosing whether to treat something as settled or as still open

point_json.grammar_name: What the first conditional does: warning, promise, offer, negotiation, argument

teach.can_do: I can warn, promise, offer and argue by saying what follows from something, and show whether I think it is settled.
teach.why_it_matters: The form is easy and the choice is not. Using when for something you cannot know turns an arguable point into a claim a reader will not accept.
teach.meaning: This shape does far more than describe the future. Attach a consequence to a condition and you have a warning, a promise, an offer, an opening bid in a negotiation, or the backbone of an argument, depending on who the consequence lands on and whether they want it. The one word you have to get right is the one at the front. If leaves the condition open and hands the other person a real choice. When closes it and says the only question left is the timing.

form.pattern: If / When + present form, will + verb
notes: If keeps the condition open. When treats it as certain and only leaves the timing unsettled.
Neither word lets will into its own half, however far into the future the sentence reaches.
The job the sentence does comes from who the consequence lands on: a consequence the listener wants is an offer, one they do not want is a warning, and one you control is a promise.
form.negative: If the yard is not clear by six, nothing will get loaded before morning.
form.question: What will you do if the inspectors turn up on Thursday?

rungs.text: If you send the figures today, I'll have the draft ready by Friday. — an offer
If we drop the delivery charge, will you take the whole batch? — a negotiation
If the yard is still blocked at six, nothing gets loaded tonight. — a warning
If the charge comes in, traffic through the village will fall. — an argument

spec.top_label: the consequence is something they want
spec.bottom_label: the consequence is something they do not want

worked_example.sentence: If the committee agrees on Thursday, we will start advertising the post the same week.
worked_example.why_this_form: The writer does not know how the vote will go and says so by leaving the condition open. What follows is an offer of speed, not a boast about it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with when would tell the committee that their agreement is already assumed, which reads as pressure and invites somebody to disagree just to prove it is not.

notice_set.sentence: If the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker expecting the inspectors?
notice_set.why: Leaving the visit open is how the speaker says nobody has confirmed it.

notice_set.sentence: When the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker expecting the inspectors?
notice_set.why: The visit has been treated as settled, so the only thing left in doubt is the hour.

notice_set.sentence: If you send the figures across today, I will have the draft ready by Friday.
notice_set.question: Who benefits from the second half of this sentence?
notice_set.why: The consequence is something the listener wants, which is what makes the sentence an offer rather than a threat.

notice_set.sentence: If the yard is still blocked at six, nothing will get loaded before morning.
notice_set.question: Who is likely to be unhappy about the second half?
notice_set.why: Exactly the same shape, but the consequence now lands on the listener as something to avoid, which turns it into a warning.

notice_set.sentence: If we drop the delivery charge, will you take the whole batch?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving something away or asking for something?
notice_set.why: A concession has been tied to a request in one sentence, which is what bargaining sounds like in English.

discovery.prompt: Each pair changes one word at the front. Work out what that word does to the rest of the sentence.
pairs: If the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
When the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
If the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
When the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
If the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.
When the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.

candidate_rules.text: If leaves the first half open; when says it is settled and only the timing is unknown.
When is used for things that happen soon and if for things further away.
Use when whenever the sentence names a day, and if when it does not.

teach.rule_line: If hands the other person a choice. When tells them the decision is already made.
teach.false_rule: That if and when are interchangeable in a sentence about the future. Swapping them does not change the timing; it changes what you are claiming to know.

contrast.question: Is the first half settled, or could it still go either way?

fork.answer: It could still go either way, and the other person can affect it
It is going to happen; only the hour or the date is unsettled

a.text: If the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
a.means: The reopening is still in doubt. The writer is showing what would be gained by it.

b.text: When the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
b.means: The reopening is going ahead. The writer is telling you what to expect once it does.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote when. That tells your reader the tunnel is definitely reopening and that you know it. If it is still a proposal, you have just claimed something you cannot support, and a reader who spots it stops trusting the rest of the paragraph.

edge_case.text: In a warm invitation, when is used on purpose for something that is not settled at all: come and see us when you are next over. The speaker is being generous about the odds, not reporting them. Recognise it and leave it out of an essay.

contrast.stronger_test: Put the words as far as I know in front of the first half. If the sentence now sounds contradictory, you needed if. If it sounds merely modest, when was fine.

worked_pairs.a: If the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.
worked_pairs.b: When the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first was written by somebody waiting to hear. The second was written by somebody who has already had the letter.

worked_pairs.b: When the appeal is heard, the family will find out about the flat.

worked_pairs.b: When councils charge for parking in the centre, small shops lose their regulars.

errors.wrong: When the appeal succeeds, the family will move back into the flat.
errors.right: If the appeal succeeds, the family will move back into the flat.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer wants the appeal to succeed and lets the hope into the grammar. When reports the outcome as settled, which is a claim nobody has made and nobody can support.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: When becomes If.

errors.wrong: When the results will come out in August, we will know whether the course runs.
errors.right: When the results come out in August, we will know whether the course runs.
errors.why_it_happens: August is clearly ahead, so the future gets marked twice. English marks it once and leaves the half that fixes the moment in a plain present form, exactly as it does after if.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: If the inspection is confirmed for Thursday, we'd move the vans out of the yard.
errors.right: If the inspection is confirmed for Thursday, we'll move the vans out of the yard.

pays_in.model: If the charge is introduced across the whole county, smaller towns will lose their bus links first.

pays_in.note: Arrangements are announced with when and warnings with if, and the difference carries the answer.

feedback.why_key: March is ahead of us, but the half that fixes the moment stays plain. Only the promise takes will.

payload.context: A driver offering to help a colleague who has no lift home.

feedback.why_key: The consequence is something the listener wants, and a firm form is what makes it an offer rather than a musing.
feedback.feed_forward: Use will for a promise you intend to keep.

payload.given: The council is thinking about scrapping bus fares. Nobody has voted yet. The writer expects passenger numbers to double.

scraps bus fares, passenger numbers will double

scraps the fares, passenger numbers will double

feedback.feed_forward: Open with if whenever the decision has not been taken.

payload.audio_text: When the audit's over, they'll tell us about the second shift.

expected: when the audit's over they'll tell us about the second shift
when the audit is over they will tell us about the second shift
when the audits over theyll tell us about the second shift

feedback.why_key: When and if are both single unstressed syllables at speed, and mishearing one for the other reverses what the speaker claims to know.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen hard to the first word of a two-part sentence.

payload.context: From a residents' newsletter about a building already under contract.
payload.stem: When work ___ (begin) on the old mill in April, the lane will be closed to traffic for six weeks.

feedback.why_key: The contract is signed, so the start is settled and the sentence is telling residents what to expect around it.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the moment with a plain verb and predict with will.

items.decision_cue: the day the appeal was lodged

payload.sentence: When the appeal succeeds, the family will move back into the flat above the shop.

the family does not want to move back
the second half should be in a present form
nothing wrong, it's fine

options.why_this_means: That the money is still in doubt and the hiring is a plan for one of two futures.

points.title: Signalling that what you are describing is not the case

point_json.grammar_name: The unreal past: one step back means one step away from reality

teach.can_do: I can show that I am describing something that is not the case, without saying so.
teach.why_it_matters: This one move is behind six different structures. Learn it here and the rest of the unit costs almost nothing.
teach.meaning: English has a quiet way of saying this is not so. You move the verb one step further back than the time you are actually talking about. I know her name is a report about now. I wish I knew her name is also about now, but the backward step tells the listener that the knowing is missing. The step is not about time at all. It is distance from what is true, and once you can see it you will start seeing it everywhere: in wishes, in regrets, in advice, in polite requests, and in every sentence about a world the speaker is only imagining.

form.pattern: one step further back than the time you actually mean
notes: About now or about the future, take a step back to the past simple: I wish I lived nearer the coast.
About the past, take a step back to had plus the past participle: I wish I had asked her at the time.
Were is available for every subject inside these sentences: I wish it were simpler. Was is also very common in speech and nobody will stop you.
The step happens after wish, if only, it's time, would rather, suppose and imagine, and it is what powers the two shapes coming next in this unit.
form.negative: The step survives a negative without changing: I wish I didn't have to drive in every day.
form.question: Would it help if I sent the figures over this afternoon?

marks.label: I know her name — plain present form
I wish I knew her name — a step back, still about now
I wish I had known her name — two steps back, about that evening

worked_example.sentence: I wish the shop took cards, because I never carry cash any more.
worked_example.why_this_form: The speaker is talking about the shop as it is today. Took, rather than takes, is the whole message: the card machine does not exist, and that is what is being complained about.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: I wish the shop takes cards is not a gentler way of making the same complaint. It leaves the listener with no signal that the machine is missing, and the sentence falls apart.

notice_set.sentence: I wish the shop took cards.
notice_set.question: Can you pay by card in that shop?
notice_set.why: The backward step is the speaker's way of saying the card machine is not there.

notice_set.sentence: I wish I had asked her about the deposit at the time.
notice_set.question: Did the speaker ask about the deposit?
notice_set.why: Two steps back reaches an occasion that is over, and says the asking did not happen on it.

notice_set.sentence: It's time we left for the airport.
notice_set.question: Have they left yet?
notice_set.why: Left points at a departure that has not taken place, and the sentence is a nudge to make it take place now.

notice_set.sentence: I'd rather you didn't mention the figures until Monday.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker want the figures mentioned today?
notice_set.why: The step back keeps the request off the table as a demand and puts it forward as a preference instead.

notice_set.sentence: I was wondering whether you had a few minutes this afternoon.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about this afternoon or about earlier today?
notice_set.why: Nothing here is in the past. The step back is doing politeness, putting a little space between the speaker and the ask.

discovery.prompt: The left-hand and right-hand sentences are both about today. Work out what the change of verb is telling you.
pairs: The shop takes cards.
I wish the shop took cards.
We are leaving for the airport.
It's time we left for the airport.
Do you have a few minutes?
I was wondering whether you had a few minutes.

candidate_rules.text: The step backwards marks distance from what is true, not distance in time.
The right-hand sentences are about things the speaker regrets.
A verb in a past form always means the event happened before now.

teach.rule_line: Move the verb one step back and the listener hears: this is not the case.
teach.false_rule: That a past form always means past time. Here it means distance from reality, and the sentence can be about this afternoon.

errors.wrong: I wish I know more about how the scheme is funded.
errors.right: I wish I knew more about how the scheme is funded.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence is about now, so a present form arrives on time and sounds right. The learner has never been told that the backward step is what carries the meaning, so nothing stops it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: know becomes knew.

errors.wrong: I wish I would have asked about the deposit at the time.
errors.right: I wish I had asked about the deposit at the time.
errors.why_it_happens: Would has been learned as the marker of an imagined world, so it is added to make the sentence sound unreal. The step backwards has already done that job, and would jams a second signal on top of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would have asked becomes had asked.
errors.l1_note: Speakers of several languages hear this version regularly in informal English, which keeps it alive.

errors.wrong: I'd rather you don't mention the figures until Monday.
errors.right: I'd rather you didn't mention the figures until Monday.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reads would rather as a polite way of saying please, and a polite request naturally takes a present form. The structure asks for the step back on the second verb, not the first.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: don't becomes didn't.

pays_in.note: Part 3 keeps asking about worlds that do not exist, and this is how English marks them.
pays_in.model: I wish public transport were reliable enough that people gave up their second car.

pays_in.note: Softening a request or an opinion in Part 1 runs on exactly this step.
pays_in.model: I was wondering whether there was somewhere quiet to work near the flat.

pays_in.note: Any argument about what ought to change needs a way of marking the imagined version.
pays_in.model: It is high time councils treated cycle lanes as roads rather than as decoration.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card describes something that did not happen, which is this step used over and over.
A solution paragraph is a description of a world that does not exist yet, and it needs a way of saying so.

payload.sentence: I wish the corner shop took cards.
payload.question: Can you pay by card there?

feedback.why_key: The backward step is the whole message. It says the card machine is not there, and that is what the speaker minds.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a step backwards as a claim about what is missing now.

payload.sentence: I wish I had asked about the deposit before I signed anything.
payload.question: Where does this sit?
options: something that did not happen at a moment now past
something that is not happening now

feedback.why_key: Two steps back reaches an occasion that is over and tells you the asking did not take place on it.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the steps back to find which moment is being reported as missing.

payload.context: Talking about how often she gets home to see her grandmother.
payload.sentence: I wish I have more time with my grandmother.
reasons: a wish about now needs the verb a step further back
the grandmother is no longer alive
wish cannot be used about people
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Without the step back, nothing in the sentence says the time is missing, and the complaint quietly disappears.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back whenever wish comes in front of it.

payload.context: A commuter grumbling about the last bus of the evening.
payload.stem: I wish the last bus ___ (run) half an hour later than it does.

feedback.why_key: The timetable is a fact about today, and the step back is how the speaker says it is the wrong fact.
feedback.feed_forward: Take one step back for anything you are wishing about now.

payload.context: From a note written at the end of a course.
payload.stem: If only I ___ (start) the reading list in September rather than in January.

feedback.why_key: September is over, so the step goes one further back than the past and lands on a September that never happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Use had plus the participle when the missed moment is already past.

payload.context: A manager glancing at the clock during a long meeting.
payload.stem: It's high time we ___ (move) on to the budget.

feedback.why_key: Nobody has moved on yet, and the step back is what turns a description into a nudge.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back after it's time and let the impatience do the rest.

payload.given: Please don't send the figures round until Monday.
payload.instruction: Say the same thing as a preference rather than an instruction, using would rather.

expected: didn't send the figures round until monday
did not send the figures round until monday
didnt send the figures round until monday

feedback.why_key: The step back lifts the sentence off the table as an order and puts it forward as something the listener may still refuse.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the second verb back and leave would rather alone.

payload.given: Do you have the account details somewhere?
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so it sounds less direct, keeping it about right now.

feedback.why_key: Nothing in this sentence is about the past. The step back is buying the listener room to say no.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back to make an ask easier to refuse.

payload.audio_text: I'd rather we left before the traffic builds up.

expected: i'd rather we left before the traffic builds up
i would rather we left before the traffic builds up
id rather we left before the traffic builds up

feedback.why_key: The 'd is a single consonant riding on the pronoun, and a listener who loses it hears a report about a journey already taken.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a d on the pronoun before the main verb.

payload.context: From a letter about a flat the writer turned down two years ago.
payload.sentence: I wish I would have taken the flat above the bakery when it was offered.
reasons: the step backwards already marks this as unreal, so would has no work left
the flat is still available
wish cannot be used about the past at all
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two signals for one meaning is one too many, and the second one is the one that sounds wrong to a reader.
feedback.feed_forward: Use had plus the participle after wish about the past.

payload.sentence: It is high time councils treat cycle lanes as roads rather than as decoration.

feedback.why_key: The councils are not doing it, which is the writer's whole complaint, and the step backwards is where that complaint lives.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back after it is high time.

payload.prompt_text: Think of one thing about where you live that you would change tomorrow if you could. Write one sentence saying you want it changed, without saying the words I want.

feedback.why_key: The step backwards is doing something no other part of the sentence can do: it says the thing is not so, while the sentence talks about now.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what is not the case by stepping the verb back once.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked whether a bad decision teaches a person more than a good one. In forty-five seconds, describe one choice you would take differently, marking clearly that you did not take it that way.

feedback.why_key: Speaking about a decision you did not take is the commonest place this step is needed and the commonest place it is dropped under pressure.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for had plus the participle when the moment has gone.

points.title: Describing a situation that is not the case and what would follow from it

point_json.grammar_name: Second conditional: the unreal present and future

teach.can_do: I can build a situation that is not true and say what would come out of it.
teach.why_it_matters: Half of every discussion question asks about a world that does not exist. Without this you can only describe the world that does.
teach.meaning: You already have the step backwards from the last lesson. Here it goes inside an if half, and the result half answers it with would. The whole sentence sets up a situation the speaker does not expect: the city has no tram, the fares are not free, you are not me. Nothing in it is a prediction. It is an experiment run out loud, and the listener understands from the very first verb that they are being shown a world rather than told about this one.

form.pattern: If + the step-back form, would + verb
notes: Could and might take the place of would when the result is less certain: if the fares were free, more people might walk into town instead.
In speech would collapses to 'd and is easy to miss altogether.
Were is normal for every subject inside the if half: if the site were closer to the station. Was is common in speech and nobody will correct you for it.
The halves swap freely: nobody would use the car park if the tram ran until midnight.
form.negative: If the council did not own the land, nothing would get built on it at all.
form.question: What would happen if the tram ran until midnight?

marks.label: If the tram runs until midnight, fewer people will drive. — a live proposal
If the tram ran until midnight, fewer people would drive. — a world being shown

worked_example.sentence: If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic through the centre would disappear.
worked_example.why_this_form: The tram stops at eleven and the speaker has no reason to think that is changing. Ran and would disappear together tell the listener the whole sentence is a picture, not a forecast.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: If the tram runs until midnight, half the traffic will disappear would tell a councillor that the later service is genuinely on the table and that the speaker is arguing for a decision, not painting one.

notice_set.sentence: If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic would disappear.
notice_set.question: Does the tram run until midnight?
notice_set.why: The step backwards in the first half is the speaker's way of saying the late service does not exist.

notice_set.sentence: If I lived nearer the depot, I would walk in every morning.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker walk to work?
notice_set.why: The walking is tied to a house the speaker does not live in, so it is not happening either.

notice_set.sentence: If bus fares were free, town centres might fill up again on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: How sure is the speaker about the Saturday crowds?
options: Treating it as possible rather than certain
notice_set.why: Might in place of would keeps the result loose, and the speaker is showing a world without promising what it contains.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody would use the multi-storey if parking on the street were free.
notice_set.question: Is street parking free at the moment?
notice_set.why: The signal sits in the second half of the sentence here, but it says exactly the same thing about the world.

notice_set.sentence: If the council did not own that land, nothing would get built on it at all.
notice_set.question: Who owns the land?
notice_set.why: A negative inside an unreal half flips the world twice: the sentence supposes away an ownership that really exists.

discovery.prompt: Both sentences in each pair are about the same town. Work out which speaker expects something to change.
pairs: If the tram runs until midnight, half the late-night traffic will disappear.
If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic would disappear.
If bus fares are free, town centres will fill up on Saturdays.
If bus fares were free, town centres would fill up on Saturdays.
If I live nearer the depot, I will walk in every morning.
If I lived nearer the depot, I would walk in every morning.

candidate_rules.text: The right-hand speaker is showing a world that is not the case; the left-hand speaker is arguing about a real decision.
The right-hand sentences are about things that are impossible.
Would is the polite version of will, so the right-hand sentences are simply more formal.

teach.rule_line: Step the if half back, answer it with would, and the listener knows none of it is so.
teach.false_rule: That this shape is for the future and the last one was for the present. Both can be about tomorrow; only one of them expects tomorrow to look like that.

errors.wrong: If the council would ban cars from the centre, air quality would improve within a year.
errors.right: If the council banned cars from the centre, air quality would improve within a year.
errors.why_it_happens: Would is the most visible sign that a sentence is imaginary, so the learner puts it in both halves to make sure the reader sees it. English marks the world once and marks it in the answering half.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would ban becomes banned.

errors.wrong: If the city built a tram line, congestion will fall by a third.
errors.right: If the city built a tram line, congestion would fall by a third.
errors.why_it_happens: The two halves are written a few seconds apart and only the first one gets thought about. By the time the writer reaches the result they are predicting again, and the sentence ends up in two worlds at once.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will fall becomes would fall.

errors.wrong: If fares were free, far more people would to use the evening buses.
errors.right: If fares were free, far more people would use the evening buses.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is treating would like an ordinary verb, and ordinary verbs take to in front of the next one. Would belongs to a small family that refuses it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

pays_in.note: What would happen if is a Part 3 question type, and the answer must match the question.
pays_in.model: If cities charged drivers by the mile, people would think much harder about short journeys.

pays_in.note: A counter-argument often runs on a world the writer does not expect to arrive.
pays_in.model: If universities dropped their entry tests, admissions offices would have nothing left to compare.

pays_in.note: A speaker weighing options in Part 3 marks each imagined one this way.
pays_in.model: If we moved the session to the annexe, we would lose the projector.

used_in.quote: The follow-ups ask what a town would look like under conditions that do not hold, and the grammar has to say so.
The strongest paragraphs describe a centre without cars, which is a place that does not exist yet.

payload.sentence: If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic through the centre would disappear.
payload.question: Does the tram run until midnight?

feedback.why_key: The step backwards in the first half says the late service does not exist, and the whole sentence is a picture of a town that would be different if it did.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a stepped-back if half as a claim about what is missing.

payload.sentence: If I lived nearer the depot, I'd walk in every morning.
payload.question: How does the speaker get to work at the moment?

feedback.why_key: The walking is tied to a house the speaker does not live in, so it is not happening either. The sentence never says what she does instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow the imagined half through to what it cancels.

payload.context: From a paragraph imagining a city with no private cars at all.
payload.sentence: If the city banned cars from the centre altogether, emissions will fall by a third within a year.
reasons: the two halves disagree about whether any of this is expected

points.title: Choosing whether to argue about a real decision or show an imagined one

point_json.grammar_name: Using the unreal present: advice, softened requests and imagined policy

teach.can_do: I can pick between arguing about something that may really happen and showing something that will not.
teach.why_it_matters: Both shapes are correct English and only one is honest about what you know. Get it wrong and a firm plan sounds idle, or a stray thought sounds binding.
teach.meaning: The two shapes you now have look similar and claim opposite things. The plain one puts a real decision on the table and argues about it: somebody could still act on your sentence. The stepped-back one takes the decision off the table and shows a picture instead: nobody is expected to act, and that is precisely why it is safe to use for advice, for softening what you want, and for the imagined worlds a discussion question keeps asking about. Choosing between them is choosing what you are claiming to know.

form.pattern: If + present form, will + verb   OR   If + step-back form, would + verb
notes: The two halves move together. Stepping the first half back and leaving will in the second is the single commonest wreck in this unit.
If I were you is fixed advice, and nobody expects the listener to become the speaker. The stepped-back form is what makes it advice rather than an order.
It would help if you could send the figures is a request, not a hypothesis. The step back is buying the other person room to refuse.
form.negative: If the funding did not run out in June, none of this would be urgent.
form.question: What would you do if you were running the department?

left.role: on the table: somebody could act on this
left.text: If the college drops the evening slot, working students will have to travel in.

right.role: off the table: a picture, or a piece of advice
right.text: If the college dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel in.

spec.caption: Same college, same students. Only one of these sentences is asking anybody to do anything.

notice_set.question: Does the speaker expect the listener to become the speaker?
notice_set.why: Nobody takes this half literally. The impossible opening is what makes the second half advice rather than an instruction.

notice_set.question: Is the speaker describing an imaginary situation or asking for something?
notice_set.why: This is a request wearing the clothes of a hypothesis. The step backwards leaves the listener room to say no.

candidate_rules.text: The left-hand sentences treat the decision as live; the right-hand ones show a picture nobody is expected to act on.
The right-hand sentences are the polite ones, so they belong in formal writing.
Would is used for the more distant future and will for the nearer one.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether anybody could act on your sentence. If nobody could, step it back.
teach.false_rule: That the stepped-back version is just the polite one. Politeness is a side effect; the sentence is claiming that none of this is expected to happen.

contrast.question: Could anybody actually act on this sentence?

fork.answer: Yes, the decision is live and somebody is weighing it right now
No, I am showing a picture, giving advice, or softening a request

a.text: If the firm wins the Ashfield contract, we will take on four more drivers.
a.means: The bid is in and the result is coming. Four people may genuinely be hired.

b.text: If the firm won the Ashfield contract, we would take on four more drivers.
b.means: The firm is not going to win it. The four drivers are a way of saying how big the contract is.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You stepped it back. To a manager reading it, that says the bid is hopeless and the hiring plan is a daydream. If the tender is genuinely open, you have just told your own team not to bother preparing for it.

edge_case.text: A speaker sometimes steps a live possibility back on purpose, to be modest or to avoid jinxing it: if we won it, we'd need four more drivers, said by somebody who thinks the bid is strong. Hear it, enjoy it, and keep it out of an essay where the reader cannot see your face.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask what the sentence would sound like if the person who takes the decision were standing behind you. If it would embarrass you to be overheard treating their decision as already lost, you needed the plain forms.

worked_pairs.b: If the mill site were cleared, forty homes would go up on it.

errors.wrong: If I were in charge of the budget, I will spend it on the evening classes.
errors.right: If I were in charge of the budget, I would spend it on the evening classes.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening is a fixed phrase the learner has memorised whole, so it comes out right without being thought about. The second half is built from scratch a moment later, and the default for a future statement is will.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will spend becomes would spend.

errors.wrong: If the college would drop the evening slot, working students would have to travel in.
errors.right: If the college dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel in.
errors.why_it_happens: Both halves are imagined, so the learner marks both. The result is a sentence that reads as a complaint about whether the college is willing, rather than a picture of what would follow.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would drop becomes dropped.

errors.wrong: If I were you, I must ask for the figures in writing.
errors.right: If I were you, I would ask for the figures in writing.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner wants the advice to sound serious and reaches for the strongest word available. Must turns a suggestion into an order and cancels the softening the opening phrase was chosen for.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: must becomes would.

points.title: Describing a past that did not happen and what would have followed from it

teach.can_do: I can describe a past that did not happen and say what would have come out of it.
teach.why_it_matters: It is how you criticise a decision without blaming anybody, and how you show you have thought about what else could have been done.
teach.meaning: This is the same step backwards you already know, applied to a moment that is over. The past is fixed, so to move away from it you have to go one place further back than the past itself. The sentence then runs a different version of an afternoon that has already been and gone: the survey was started late, the ward stayed open, the letter never arrived. Nobody is being told what to do. The speaker is showing an alternative history, usually because it explains something about the one we got.

form.pattern: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle
notes: Could have and might have take the place of would have when the outcome is less certain: the ward might have stayed open.
In speech both halves shrink: the first 'd is had and the second is would, and would have becomes something close to would've. Two different words end up sounding almost the same.
The halves swap freely, and when the result comes first no comma is needed.
form.negative: If the letter had not gone to the wrong address, none of this would have happened.
form.question: What would have happened if the survey had started in March?

marks.label: the survey started in June — what really happened
a March start — the version that did not happen
no flooding — what would have followed

spec.caption: Two histories running side by side. Only one of them left anybody wet.

worked_example.sentence: If the drainage survey had started in March, the flooding on the estate would have been picked up in time.
worked_example.why_this_form: The survey started in June and the estate flooded. Both halves reach one step behind the past, which is how the speaker builds a spring that never existed without accusing anybody of anything.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: If the survey started in March, the flooding would be picked up in time reads as a rule about surveys in general, and the estate that actually flooded disappears from the sentence entirely.

notice_set.sentence: If the drainage survey had started in March, the flooding would have been picked up in time.
notice_set.question: Was there flooding?
notice_set.why: The second half describes a rescue that did not happen, which tells you the thing it would have prevented did.

notice_set.why: A negative inside an unreal half supposes away something that really happened, so the letter did go astray and the appointment was lost.

notice_set.question: Is the speaker blaming a particular person?
notice_set.why: The criticism is aimed at a decision rather than at whoever took it, which is why this shape survives in a report that has to be read by everybody.

The right-hand sentences are the ones expressing regret.

teach.rule_line: To move away from a past that is fixed, go one step further back than the past.
teach.false_rule: That this shape is only for regret. It is just as often used to analyse a decision, and the speaker may have no feelings about it whatsoever.

errors.why_it_happens: The result half needs three words in a row before the main verb and the middle one carries no meaning a learner can hear, so it drops out first when the sentence is being built at speed.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: have.

errors.wrong: If the council would have consulted residents, the plan would have gone through.

errors.why_it_happens: Both halves describe things that did not happen, so the learner marks both the same way. English marks the supposing half with had and saves would for the answering half.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would have consulted becomes had consulted.
errors.l1_note: This version is common in casual speech in some places, which keeps it in circulation.

teach.meaning: Everything you have built so far matched its two halves: both real, both imagined about now, both imagined about the past. Real situations are not that tidy. A decision taken badly in 2015 is often the reason a street is jammed this week, and a fact about you that has not changed is often the reason an offer went elsewhere last spring. When the two halves sit in different times, you mark each half for its own time and leave them unmatched. That is not an exception to the system. point_json.grammar_name: unless, provided that, as long as, in case, even if, otherwise, supposing

teach.can_do: I can name the single thing that would stop something, or say that nothing would.
teach.why_it_matters: If is a blunt instrument. These words say how much weight the condition carries, and one of them means the opposite of what most learners think.
teach.meaning: If simply attaches a condition. The words in this lesson say what kind of condition it is. Unless names one exception to something that otherwise holds: everything is fine except in this case. Provided that and as long as name the one thing that has to be true, and refuse everything else. In case names a precaution against something that may never happen. Even if says the condition changes nothing at all. Otherwise stands at the front of a second sentence and means if that does not happen. Picking the wrong one does not sound clumsy; it says something different.

form.pattern: unless / provided that / as long as / in case / even if + present form, and the main half as normal
notes: Unless already carries a negative inside it, so a second not turns the sentence inside out.
In case is not the same as if. Take a torch in case the lights fail means take it now, before anything has happened.
Otherwise starts a new sentence and looks back at the one before it: book by Friday, otherwise the group rate goes.
Supposing and suppose open a question rather than a statement, and are almost only spoken: supposing the ferry is cancelled, what then?

edge_case.text: Unless is not a spare part for if not. errors.wrong: Unless the tide does not turn before six, we will not get off the island.
errors.right: Unless the tide turns before six, we will not get off the island.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored unless as a translation of if not and writes out the not as well, without noticing that the word already contains one. Two negatives turn the warning inside out.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: not.

errors.wrong: The trip will run even if fewer than eight people sign up, so the centre has set a minimum of eight.
errors.right: The trip will run unless fewer than eight people sign up, so the centre has set a minimum of eight.
errors.why_it_happens: Both words attach a condition the writer would rather avoid, so the nearest one gets picked. They point in opposite directions: one cancels the result and the other refuses to.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: even if becomes unless.

errors.wrong: Provided that the weather would hold, we will finish the survey by Friday.
errors.right: Provided that the weather holds, we will finish the survey by Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: Provided that looks formal, so the learner reaches for a more elaborate verb to match it. It behaves exactly like if, and the half after it stays plain however grand the connecting words are.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would hold becomes holds.

pays_in.note: A letter that sets terms needs the exact weight of each condition.
pays_in.model: The deposit is returned in full provided that the keys are handed back by noon.

pays_in.note: True and false stems turn on whether a condition is an exception or a requirement.
pays_in.model: Visitors may walk the ridge all year unless the reserve is closed for nesting.

pays_in.note: Conceding a point out loud is usually done with even if, and it costs nothing.
pays_in.model: Even if the museum charged for entry, most people would still go once a year.

used_in.quote: A complaint that states what would put the matter right has to say exactly how much weight that condition carries.
The notices in this section are built from conditions, and getting the exception the wrong way round loses the question.

payload.sentence: The crossing runs twice a day all winter unless the wind gets up.
payload.question: Can you expect a boat on a calm January morning?

feedback.why_key: One exception has been named, which means everything outside that exception leaves the timetable exactly as it stands.
feedback.feed_forward: Read unless as naming the only thing that stops it.

payload.sentence: Bring your boots in case the pitch is soft.
payload.question: Is the pitch soft?

feedback.why_key: Nothing has happened yet. This is a precaution taken now against something that may never come.
feedback.feed_forward: Read in case as pack it before you find out.

payload.context: From a notice at the top of the causeway.
payload.sentence: Unless the tide does not turn before six, you will not get back across.
reasons: unless already carries a negative, and a second one turns the warning inside out
the tide never turns before six
a notice cannot use the word unless
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: As written, the notice promises the walk back only on days when the tide stays out, which reverses the warning it was meant to give.
feedback.feed_forward: Take the not out when you have already written unless.

payload.context: From the terms sent out with a group booking.
payload.stem: The group rate holds provided that everyone ___ (book) by Friday.

feedback.why_key: Provided that behaves exactly like if, however formal it looks, and the half after it stays plain.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the verb plain after provided that.

payload.context: A guide talking to a walking group at the bottom of the causeway.
payload.stem: Unless the tide ___ (turn) before six, we're staying on the island tonight.

feedback.why_key: The negative is already sitting inside unless, so the verb after it stays positive and plain.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the verb after unless without a not.

payload.given: The coach leaves at seven. If you are not at the harbour by ten to, it goes without you.
payload.instruction: Write the second part as one sentence beginning with otherwise, so it looks back at the first.
payload.starter: Be at the harbour by ten to seven. Otherwise ___

expected: the coach will go without you

feedback.why_key: Otherwise carries the whole negative condition on its own, so nothing from the first sentence has to be repeated.
feedback.feed_forward: Start the second sentence with otherwise and say only the consequence.

payload.audio_text: We'll be on the six o'clock boat unless the harbour's closed.

expected: we'll be on the six o'clock boat unless the harbour's closed
we will be on the six o'clock boat unless the harbour is closed
we will be on the six oclock boat unless the harbour is closed
well be on the six oclock boat unless the harbours closed

feedback.why_key: Unless goes by in a single unstressed beat, and a listener who hears if instead takes away the opposite arrangement.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the second syllable of the connecting word.

payload.context: From a letter about a place on a course.
payload.sentence: I would be very surprised unless she accepted the offer.
reasons: the condition is a reaction rather than an exception, and unless will not go there
surprise cannot be conditional
the offer has already been accepted
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here holds by default with one exception carved out of it. The writer is reporting how they would react, which needs if not.
feedback.feed_forward: Test it with except if before you write unless.

payload.sentence: Provided that the weather would hold, the survey team will finish the last two inlets by Friday.

feedback.why_key: Provided that is only a formal-looking if, and the half after it takes the same plain verb it always did.
feedback.feed_forward: Do not dress up the verb to match the connecting words.

items.decision_cue: the single reason young families give for leaving

payload.context: A survey found that the two-hour crossing is the single reason young families give for leaving the island.
payload.stem: ___ the ferry timetable improves, the island will keep losing families.

options.why_this_means: That the timetable is the one thing that would stop the losses.
That the timetable makes no difference and the families will go anyway.

feedback.why_key: The survey names the crossing as the cause, so fixing it is the exception that would leave the island standing.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the single exception when one thing is doing the damage.

payload.context: A survey found that families leave because there is no secondary school on the island, and the crossing barely came up at all.
payload.stem: ___ the ferry timetable improves, the island will keep losing families.

options.why_this_means: That the timetable is the one thing that would stop the losses.
That the timetable makes no difference and the families will go anyway.

feedback.why_key: The boats are not the problem, so promising that better boats would fix it would be an argument nobody on the island would recognise.
feedback.feed_forward: Concede the condition when it is not the cause.

items.decision_cue: eight is the minimum that covers it

payload.context: The centre hires a coach for the walking trip at a fixed price, and the organiser has said eight is the minimum that covers it.
payload.stem: The trip will run ___ fewer than eight people sign up.

options.why_this_means: That low numbers are the one thing that would cancel it.
That low numbers change nothing and the trip goes ahead regardless.

feedback.why_key: A fixed coach price with a stated minimum is exactly the shape of a single exception, and everything above eight leaves the trip standing.
feedback.feed_forward: Use unless when one named shortfall would cancel it.

items.decision_cue: promised to the group since Easter, whatever the numbers

payload.context: The centre owns a minibus, and the walking trip has been promised to the group since Easter, whatever the numbers.
payload.stem: The trip will run ___ fewer than eight people sign up.

options.why_this_means: That low numbers are the one thing that would cancel it.
That low numbers change nothing and the trip goes ahead regardless.

feedback.why_key: A promise made at Easter and a minibus in the yard mean the numbers decide nothing at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Concede a condition that cannot change the outcome.

items.decision_cue: the organisers have not said which way they will go

payload.context: The stalls have canvas roofs, but the cobbles flood in heavy rain, and the organisers have not said which way they will go.
payload.stem: The market will be held in the square ___ the cobbles flood.

options.why_this_means: That flooding is the one thing that moves the market indoors.
That the market stays in the square whatever the cobbles are like.

follow_up.question: Which version promises stallholders the square whatever the weather does?

feedback.why_key: Both are honest notices about the same market, and stallholders would pack very differently depending on which one they read.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide how much you are promising before you choose.

items.decision_cue: two different years on the same coast path

payload.context: Two notices from two different years on the same coast path.
sentences: The path stays open all winter as long as the cliff edge is checked each month.
The path stays open all winter unless the cliff edge starts to move.
meanings: The monthly check is what keeps it open, and a missed check closes it.
It is open by default, and only movement in the cliff would close it.

feedback.why_key: One notice puts the burden on the inspectors and the other puts it on the cliff, and a walker reading them a year apart would plan differently.
